entities.summary: Engelbert III of the Marck, Archbishop of Cologne, played a pivotal role in shaping Western Europe's religious and political landscape during the Late Middle Ages. A key figure in the Holy Roman Empire, he oversaw the appointment of numerous clergy members, including the influential Archbishop-elect of Trier, and negotiated crucial trade agreements with neighboring regions. Engelbert's leadership during the 1350s helped to stabilize the region following the devastating effects of the Black Death, which had decimated the population and led to significant economic and social upheaval. The Archbishop's legacy extended beyond his own territories, as he participated in the establishment of the Council of Basel in 1438, a gathering of European theologians and clergy that aimed to reconcile the Catholic Church with Protestant reformers. Despite his significant contributions, Engelbert's life remains somewhat enshrouded in mystery, with some sources suggesting he may have been instrumental in the composition of the 'Golden Bull of 1356', a foundational document of the Holy Roman Empire that outlined the rights and responsibilities of its rulers. His tenure as Archbishop of Cologne also saw the construction of numerous churches and monasteries, including the iconic Cologne Cathedral, which would become a symbol of the city's prosperity and spiritual vitality during the 14th century. Through his leadership and diplomatic efforts, Engelbert III of the Marck left an indelible mark on the history of Western Europe, cementing his place as one of the most important figures of the Late Middle Ages.
